description: Deploying a site: hosting, going live

screens.body: Right now your site lives on your laptop — only you can see it. Publishing (deploying) means copying those files to a server that's always online, so anyone with the address can visit. It's the difference between a sketch in your notebook and a poster on a wall.

options: Putting your files on an always-online server
Emailing your code to a friend
check.question: Publishing a website means…

screens.heading: From your laptop to the world
screens.keyPoint: Publishing copies your files to an always-online server.

screens.body: A web host is a company that rents you space on their servers. Your files live there, and their computers serve them to visitors day and night — even when your laptop is closed. For simple sites, many hosts are free; you only start paying when you need more power or features.

options: Stores your files and serves them day and night
check.question: A web host…

screens.heading: Hosting: renting space on the internet
screens.keyPoint: Hosts keep your site online around the clock.

screens.body: Nobody wants to memorize number addresses like 142.250.72.14 — so we use domain names like swiftgigs.ca. A domain is a human-friendly nickname for a server's numeric address. You rent the name from a registrar, usually paying once a year to keep it yours.

options: Renting the name from a registrar
check.question: You get a domain name by…

screens.heading: Domain names are nicknames
screens.keyPoint: Domains are memorable names rented yearly.

screens.body: DNS — the Domain Name System — is the internet's phone book. When you type a domain, DNS looks up the server's real numeric address and hands it to your browser. Without DNS, you'd need to memorize strings of numbers for every site you visit.

options: Turns domain names into server addresses
check.question: DNS does…

screens.heading: DNS: the internet's phone book
screens.keyPoint: DNS translates names into server addresses.

screens.body: Deployment tools do the copying for you. Some hosts let you drag-and-drop your files. Others connect to your Git repo: every time you push code, the site rebuilds and updates automatically — that's called push-to-deploy. The old-school way is FTP, uploading files by hand. Pick the tool that matches how you work.

options: Pushing to Git publishes your site automatically
Pushing your laptop off the desk
check.question: Push-to-deploy means…

screens.heading: Deployment tools do the copying
screens.keyPoint: Deploy by drag-and-drop, Git push, or FTP upload.

screens.body: Now the whole journey makes sense. You enter a URL. DNS turns the name into a server address. Your browser requests the files. The server sends them back. The browser builds the page. You learned the first half of this trip in 'How Websites Work' — now you know where the files actually live.

options: The browser requests the files from the server
check.question: After DNS finds the address…

screens.heading: The full journey of a visit
screens.keyPoint: URL → DNS → request → files → rendered page.

screens.body: Before you share your URL with the world, run the checklist. Click every link. Open the site on your phone — most visitors are on mobile. Make sure your custom domain is connected and the site loads over HTTPS (the little padlock). Then share it everywhere.

options: Test it on your phone and check every link
check.question: Before sharing your URL…

screens.heading: Going live checklist
screens.keyPoint: Test links, test mobile, confirm HTTPS, then share.
